slides.title: One print job must reach at most one desk
keyPoints: Labels prefer the label desk
The general desk can be a fallback
Reject invalid pages before selecting any desk
slides.narration: A print workshop has a special desk for labels and a general desk that can also handle labels. A job names a format and a page count. We need one destination, not two. Every configuration must reject a page count outside one through one thousand, and unknown formats must produce an explicit unhandled result. This example chooses a destination; it does not print pages or confirm a printer completed work. The new design pressure is that different shifts may choose different ordered sets of desks. We want to change that order without copying page validation and fallback logic into several unrelated routing functions.
actions: Ask why a label can be accepted by two desks while still receiving only one destination.
slides.sourceRef: manuscript/ch13.json → The problem: one job, one responsible desk

question.prompt: Does a returned destination prove that printing succeeded?
question.answer: No. It reports routing responsibility; actual printing and delivery failure are separate concerns.

slides.title: Fixed choices deserve a fixed direct function
keyPoints: Validate mandatory bounds first
Use clear conditions for stable choices
A changing rule set creates pressure to separate assembly
slides.narration: This complete baseline directly maps formats to destinations. It uses string_view to borrow text during the call without owning or extending that text's lifetime. Our calls pass string literals, which remain valid. The first condition checks a shared requirement before either desk is considered. With two fixed choices, this is clear and sufficient; no class hierarchy is missing. The limitation arrives when shifts need different priorities, a temporary fallback, or a new express desk. Rewriting the whole function for each shift duplicates the guard and the unhandled case. We then want the routing algorithm to stay fixed while a separately assembled ordered set supplies the decisions.
actions: Run the four inputs, then propose how a shift without a label desk would change this function.
slides.sourceRef: Lecture demonstration for manuscript/ch13.json → The problem: one job, one responsible desk

question.prompt: When is the direct if-based implementation preferable to a configurable chain?
question.answer: When the destinations and their priority are fixed and simple, so separate handlers add complexity without useful variation.

slides.title: The final assignment is not the first answer
keyPoints: Both desks can accept a label
Return stops the search immediately
Assignment followed by continuation changes the policy
slides.narration: To isolate the stop rule, this short program starts with two already-computed desk replies. Both are present because both desks can handle a label. The first function returns the first present reply. The second deliberately keeps assigning and returns only after the loop. It therefore replaces the special label destination with the general one. Both functions are well-typed, and the code runs without undefined behavior. The error is the changed routing contract. In the chapter, continuing could also call later handlers unnecessarily. If handlers performed real external work, that could be worse than a wrong name. Keep selection separate from printing so the routing decision remains easy to test.
actions: Predict first and last before running, then identify the control-flow difference.
slides.sourceRef: Lecture demonstration for manuscript/ch13.json → First-handler routing is not an all-stage pipeline

question.prompt: Why is replacing return *reply with result = *reply not an equivalent cleanup?
question.answer: The assignment continues the loop, allowing a later accepted reply to replace the first one.

slides.title: A handler answers or deliberately declines
keyPoints: Every Rule borrows the same read-only Job
A present Reply accepts responsibility
No Reply passes the request onward
slides.narration: A handler is a piece of code that decides whether it is responsible for one request. Chain of Responsibility arranges such handlers in an order and defines when to pass or stop. Our version stops at the first answer. Reply is an optional string: either one destination exists or no destination exists. No answer is a normal decline, so label_rule need not throw when it sees a report. Route then gives the next rule a chance. The shared rule shape allows assembly without forcing each handler to know its neighbor. A vector owns the order; the handlers stay focused on their own acceptance decision.
actions: Ask learners to explain decline without using the word error.
slides.sourceRef: manuscript/ch13.json → Make each choice a small, honest question

question.prompt: What happens when every handler declines a valid archive job?
question.answer: The loop finishes and route returns the explicit unhandled result.

slides.title: The contract we must preserve
keyPoints: Reject page counts outside 1 through 1000 before routing.
Choose the first willing handler; expose unsupported formats.
Allow the same handlers to be arranged in another order.
slides.narration:
Print-workshop request routing. Store small function handlers in a vector and use an optional destination. The vector makes order visible; the optional result separates a decline from an accepted request. One route function owns the stopping rule.

Reject page counts outside 1 through 1000 before routing. Choose the first willing handler; expose unsupported formats. Allow the same handlers to be arranged in another order.

A valid job receives at most one destination. Every handler sees the same unchanged job. Rejected counts never enter a handler. These are the rules that define a correct extension, even if it has the right C++ types. A direct if/else chain is clearer when the choices and their order never vary. Virtual Handler classes suit handlers with substantial private state, but would add unnecessary lifetime machinery to these two stateless rules.

question.prompt: Which promise would a new Chain of Responsibility implementation be allowed to break?
question.answer: None of the stated requirements. The implementation may change, but these rules remain: A valid job receives at most one destination. Every handler sees the same unchanged job. Rejected counts never enter a handler.

slides.title: The problem: one job, one responsible desk
keyPoints: A small print workshop receives a Job containing a format name and a page count.
For two fixed destinations, an if statement is a sound start.
slides.narration:
A small print workshop receives a Job containing a format name and a page count. Labels should go to a label desk; ordinary reports go to a general desk. The general desk can also print labels when the special desk is absent. Each job must reach at most one desk. The workshop rejects a page count below one or above one thousand before considering any desk. Unsupported formats must produce a visible unhandled result. No real printing happens in this teaching program: it chooses a destination so that routing can be checked without consuming supplies.

For two fixed destinations, an if statement is a sound start. Read the format, choose a destination, and return. There is no need to build a class family merely because several destinations exist. The limit appears when different workshop shifts need different ordered sets of rules. Copying the whole function for each shift also copies validation and fallback behavior. One shift may then accept zero-page jobs while another rejects them. We need to assemble the choices while keeping the routing contract in one place.

question.prompt: A label request matches both a label desk and a general desk. Which should receive it?
question.answer: The first willing rule in the configured order receives it. A specific rule must come before a broad rule if it should take priority. Reordering the rules can change the answer.

slides.title: Make each choice a small, honest question
keyPoints: A handler is a piece of code that accepts a request, decides whether it can handle it, and reports that decision.
Reply is std::optional<std::string>: it contains either one destination string or no string.
slides.narration:
A handler is a piece of code that accepts a request, decides whether it can handle it, and reports that decision. A chain of responsibility is an ordered set of these handlers. The delivered program represents each handler as a function. Rule is a short name, introduced by using, for std::function<Reply(const Job&)>. This standard wrapper can hold different callable objects with the same call shape. Here the shape means: borrow a read-only Job and return a Reply. The program does not need a next pointer inside every handler because a vector already stores their order.

Reply is std::optional<std::string>: it contains either one destination string or no string. std::nullopt explicitly means there is no answer here. That is different from an answer whose string happens to be empty. The if (reply) condition asks whether a value exists. The expression *reply then accesses that value; the asterisk is safe because the presence check came first. A missing answer is ordinary control flow, not an exception. The caller receives a separate text result, unhandled, only after every handler declines.

slides.title: Follow control and data through the chain
keyPoints: route first checks the page count.
For a label job, label_rule returns a value, so route returns immediately.
slides.narration:
route first checks the page count. The test uses ||, meaning that either bad bound is enough to reject the job. Valid jobs enter a range-based for loop. In for (const auto& rule : rules), the colon means take each item from rules in order. auto obtains the function-wrapper type from the vector; the reference avoids copying that wrapper; const prevents this loop from changing it. The same read-only Job is borrowed by each call. No handler owns the job, stores its address, or extends its lifetime.

For a label job, label_rule returns a value, so route returns immediately. general_rule is never called for that request. For a report, the first handler returns no value and the second supplies the destination. For archive, both decline. The compiler checks that each stored callable has the required input and result shape. Which handler supplies the answer is decided during execution from the job and the order of rules. Moving the rules into a different vector can change behavior without recompiling route, although changing the source initializer still requires rebuilding the executable.

slides.title: First-handler routing is not an all-stage pipeline
keyPoints: A pipeline is a sequence in which several stages may each perform part of the work.
Decide the rule before choosing an interface.
slides.narration:
A pipeline is a sequence in which several stages may each perform part of the work. A document pipeline might validate pages, add a tracking code, write a record, and print. Success at one stage normally means continue. Our chain has a different rule: an answer means stop. If a maintainer converts return *reply into an assignment and continues looping, the general desk can replace the label desk because both accept labels. With real printing, that same mistake could produce two copies. The word chain alone does not tell a reader which stopping rule applies.

Decide the rule before choosing an interface. In a validation pipeline, an enum such as Continue or Reject makes sense; in this router, optional destination makes sense. Mixing both meanings in one bool makes it hard to tell whether true means finished or allowed to continue. Shared requirements such as a valid page count belong before routing. A handler that is optional in one configuration must not be the only place that enforces a mandatory check. The empty-rule test proves that having no handlers remains a defined situation.

slides.title: Boundaries, costs, and a practical review
keyPoints: The handlers are pure selection functions: their result depends on the job, and they do not print, store files, or change outside data.
Before adding a rule in real software, inspect overlap, position, failure meaning, and ownership.
slides.narration:
The handlers are pure selection functions: their result depends on the job, and they do not print, store files, or change outside data. This makes order tests cheap and repeatable. With n handlers, an unsupported request makes n calls; an early match needs fewer. std::function offers runtime flexibility but may allocate when storing a large callable. For this tiny fixed router, direct calls or a table of plain function pointers can cost less. Neither performance claim should replace a measurement if routing is on a busy path.

Before adding a rule in real software, inspect overlap, position, failure meaning, and ownership. A fallback placed first can hide every special case. A rule that captures a local reference and survives that local variable can later access a dead object. The current vector stores free functions, so it has no such captured lifetime. A linked chain would also need a no-cycle rule; this vector traversal has no link cycle to create. The model deliberately omits retries and external actions. Choosing a destination successfully does not prove that the destination later completed the job.

question.prompt: What should happen if a Rule itself throws?
question.answer: The supplied route does not catch it, so the exception propagates and later handlers do not run. Continuing after failure would require an explicit error policy.

slides.title: Read the callable type from the inside out
keyPoints: Reply is optional<string>
Rule is function<Reply(const Job&)>
using introduces a readable type alias
slides.narration: Start with the call we want: a rule receives a Job and returns a Reply. The parameter const Job& borrows the existing job without changing it through that reference. Std::function can hold different callable objects that support this shape, and using gives that longer type the short name Rule. The compiler checks whether each stored callable fits. At execution, the wrapper invokes whichever callable it holds. In this chapter those are ordinary free functions, not objects with captured state. That keeps their lifetimes simple. A function-pointer table could be smaller for this exact fixed set; std::function leaves room for stateful callables if a later requirement justifies them.
actions: Read Rule aloud as “a callable from a borrowed read-only Job to a Reply.”
slides.sourceRef: manuscript/ch13.json → Make each choice a small, honest question

question.prompt: Does using Rule create a new inherited base class?
question.answer: No. It is a type alias for the callable wrapper; the chapter does not require handler inheritance.

slides.title: Presence is not the same as nonempty text
keyPoints: nullopt means no destination was supplied
An optional holding "" is still present
Check presence before dereferencing
slides.narration: Optional separates absence from the contents of a value. An empty optional means this handler declines. An optional containing an empty string still contains a value and therefore stops this router, even though that destination would be unhelpful to a person. This distinction prevents a sentinel string from doing two jobs at once. If the application requires nonempty destination names, add that as a separate invariant and validate it. The code tests if (reply) before evaluating *reply. Reversing the condition would dereference an empty optional for a decline, violating the operation's precondition. There is no defined output to predict in that incorrect program, so do not teach a guaranteed crash.
actions: Ask whether Reply{""} and std::nullopt follow the same branch.
slides.sourceRef: manuscript/ch13.json → Make each choice a small, honest question

question.prompt: Why is return *reply safe in the correct route loop?
question.answer: The immediately preceding presence test establishes that the optional contains a string.

slides.title: Order is executable policy
keyPoints: Specific rules normally precede broad fallbacks
A decline advances; an answer returns
Reordering affects overlapping acceptance sets
slides.narration: For a label job, both handlers are willing, so their order matters. With label_rule first, route returns label desk and never calls general_rule. Reverse the vector and the general desk wins immediately. For a report, the label rule declines, so the general desk still answers in either order. This is why order tests need overlapping cases, not only one request per unique format. The range-based loop visits vector entries in sequence. In const auto& rule, auto obtains the wrapper's type, the reference avoids a wrapper copy, and const prevents reassignment through that name. The colon means take each item from rules, not inheritance or a conditional expression.
actions: Predict label, report, and archive under both rule orders before revealing the chapter tests.

question.prompt: Which existing request is the strongest test of priority between the two chapter handlers?
question.answer: A label request, because both handlers accept it and the first one must win.

slides.title: Mandatory validation must survive an empty chain
keyPoints: Page bounds apply before all optional rules
Removing a handler must not remove safety
Unhandled and rejected report different facts
slides.narration: A routing rule is optional in a configuration; a mandatory input rule is not. If page validation lived only inside label_rule, a shift that removes that handler could accidentally accept zero-page reports. Route instead checks the shared bounds before touching the vector. This also gives a precise result for an empty chain: invalid input is rejected, while valid input is unhandled because no destination was available. Those outcomes should not be merged. Rejected means the request breaks an input rule; unhandled means it passed those rules but found no responsible desk. That distinction helps a caller decide whether to fix the request or change the available routing configuration.
actions: Ask for the results of zero pages with no rules and one valid page with no rules.

question.prompt: Why should the express handler not become the sole owner of the positive-page requirement?
question.answer: The handler may be omitted or reordered; a mandatory requirement must hold independently of optional routing choices.

slides.title: A router and a pipeline have different success meanings
keyPoints: Here, success means stop
In a pipeline, success may mean continue
Choose a result type that makes the rule clear
slides.narration: The word chain does not establish a stopping rule by itself. Our first-handler router stops when one destination appears. A document pipeline might validate, add a tracking number, record an event, and then print; success at each intermediate stage means continue. If a single Boolean is used in both designs, true could mean either finished or allowed to proceed. That ambiguity invites an apparently harmless refactor to change behavior. Choose a result type that expresses the actual decision. Optional destination fits this router. An enum such as Continue or Reject fits some validation pipelines. Also separate external effects from selection: retrying a destination decision is much simpler than retrying a chain that may already have printed twice.
actions: Have learners translate one routing step and one validation step into explicit result words.

question.prompt: Can a successful page validation return a destination and stop this chain?
question.answer: No. Validation establishes eligibility to route; it has not selected a desk.

slides.title: Map the roles to the actual types
keyPoints: Handler contract → Rule and Reply
Shared forwarding mechanism → route and its rules loop
Concrete handlers → label_rule and general_rule
Client and chain assembly → main and rules
slides.narration:
Handler contract → Rule and Reply. Give every handler the same input and a clear way to accept or decline. Rule is a callable contract, not an inherited base class.

Shared forwarding mechanism → route and its rules loop. Continue after a decline and detect the end. The original stores successor links; the new program stores order in one vector.

Concrete handlers → label_rule and general_rule. Apply one local acceptance rule without knowing which other rule will eventually answer.

Client and chain assembly → main and rules. Choose order and submit requests. Construction chooses policy; handlers implement the individual decisions.

The caller does not need to know the selected desk or the number of rules.
Return at once on a present answer.
slides.narration:
This loop searches for the first present reply. It runs only after the page-count guard has accepted the job. The caller does not need to know the selected desk or the number of rules.

The comment states the first-handler policy. Borrow each callable in vector order without changing it. Call that rule with the same job and store its optional reply. Check that a string is present before accessing it. Return the string and end route immediately. Close the present-reply branch. Close the loop after a decline, allowing the next rule. Return an explicit unhandled result if no rule accepted.

Return at once on a present answer. Replacing return with continued processing changes the contract into a different kind of chain.

question.prompt: Explain Chain of Responsibility without reciting its class names.
question.answer: Store small function handlers in a vector and use an optional destination. The vector makes order visible; the optional result separates a decline from an accepted request. One route function owns the stopping rule. A direct if/else chain is clearer when the choices and their order never vary. Virtual Handler classes suit handlers with substantial private state, but would add unnecessary lifetime machinery to these two stateless rules.

slides.title: An express rule extends the policy without copying the guard
keyPoints: Reports of at most five pages use express
Keep label and general behavior intact
Test overlap, boundaries, and no-handler cases
slides.narration: The lab adds an express desk for reports of up to five pages. The new rule joins a new vector before the broader existing rules, while the original vector and its checks remain intact. A five-page report now takes express; a six-page report reaches general. A label still follows label_rule, and a zero-page report is rejected before express_rule can accept it. Notice that the local express rule checks at most five, while route establishes the lower bound first. This is safe through route but matters if somebody later calls the rule directly and assumes it validates the whole request. State the boundary where the common guarantee is established.

slides.title: Runtime flexibility has lifetime and cost obligations
keyPoints: An unsupported job invokes all n handlers
Large stored callables may allocate
Captured references can outlive their targets
slides.narration: A chain trades a fixed decision tree for a configurable search. A valid unsupported job requires one call to every handler, so cost grows with the number of rules. A broad match placed early may be fast but can hide a more specific policy. Std::function may allocate when it stores a large callable, whereas this chapter's free functions are simple to retain. If you add a lambda that captures a local variable by reference, check whether the rule vector can outlive that variable. A surviving callable does not keep a borrowed capture alive. The vector avoids linked-chain cycles, but it does not solve every ownership problem a future handler might introduce.

question.prompt: Would using a vector automatically make captured references safe?
question.answer: No. The vector owns the callable wrapper, but a reference captured inside it still borrows an independently lived object.

keyPoints: Eligibility: may this job enter routing?
Responsibility: will this handler answer?
Termination: does an answer stop the search?
slides.narration: Explain this pattern through three decisions. First, the shared guard decides whether the job is eligible for routing. Second, each handler decides whether it is responsible. Third, the router decides whether to stop or continue based on the handler's result. In this chapter a present answer stops immediately; absence advances to the next rule; exhaustion produces unhandled. Those decisions remain clear even though the implementation has no linked nodes or inherited handler base. When reviewing a new rule, inspect its overlap with existing rules and its position, then test its boundary cases. The memorable mechanism is ordered responsibility with an explicit stop rule, not a required arrangement of class names.
actions: Ask learners to explain a label, an archive, and an invalid job using the three decisions.

question.prompt: What two code locations prove that this is first-handler routing?
question.answer: A handler returns nullopt to decline or a present Reply to accept, and route immediately returns the first present reply.
